Basque is a language isolate, a language with no known linguistic relatives anywhere in the world, despite centuries of scholarly investigation trying to connect it to other language families. This isolation makes it one of the most well-known living language isolates in the world. Around 700,000 people speak Basque in the Basque Country, a region spanning parts of northern Spain and southwestern France. The language stands out for its agglutinative morphology and exhibits a completely different phoneme inventory compared to the surrounding Romance languages. One of its most distinctive grammatical features is its ergative-absolutive alignment system, which differs fundamentally from the nominative-accusative system found in Romance and other Indo-European languages. Basque predates the Indo-European language expansion into Western Europe, making it a living relic of Europe's prehistoric linguistic landscape. Its origins remain hotly debated among linguists, with theories ranging from substrate remnants to possible trans-Caucasian affinities. The language faced suppression during the Franco regime but underwent a significant revival in the late twentieth century and is now co-official in the Spanish Basque Country. This revival was achieved through deliberate language preservation efforts via education and media policy.
